title: How do you decide whether a private equity fund should invest in a company?
description: "Should the fund invest in this company?" Private equity: a fund buys a company to improve it and sell it in 3 to 7 years. The structure, the first question t
hook: Private equity cases look like acquisition cases, with one important difference: the fund plans to sell in a few years, so everything comes back to whether it can make its money back several times over. Here is how to structure one.
body:
When you will use it

Private equity: a fund buys a company to improve it and sell it in 3 to 7 years.

This is a decide question: "Should we do this?" Test it against a few yes/no questions, put a number on it, and end with a clear yes or no. More on the three families of case questions.

Ask this first

What return does the fund need, over how many years?

One good question at the start can halve the work. It tells you where to look, and it shows the interviewer you are thinking about the client, not reciting a list.

The structure

  • Is the market attractive?
    • Size and growth
    • Margins
    • Barriers to entry
  • Is the company strong?
    • Position vs competitors
    • Performance and outlook
    • Management team
  • How can we add value?
    • Grow revenue
    • Raise margins
    • Buy add-on companies
  • Can we exit well? (gives the return)
    • Who would buy it
    • Exit multiple
    • Timing

Say it out loud as a short sentence per branch, then say which branch you would look at first and why. That last part, your hypothesis, is what most candidates forget.

Make it your own

Return = equity at exit ÷ equity at entry. A fund that triples its money (a 3× multiple, or MOIC) in 6 years earns about 20% a year. No credible buyer at exit means no deal.

Interviewers can tell when a structure has been memorised. Swap the general words for words about this client: not "costs", but "fuel and crew costs" for an airline.

Practise with real prompts

Read each prompt, take two minutes to sketch your own structure, then compare.

1. Should a private equity fund buy a chain of 80 gyms?

Show a model structure
  • Market: Growth, competition, low-cost vs premium; Customer churn across the industry
  • The company: Profit per gym, best vs worst; Management and membership trends
  • Value creation: New gyms, pricing, cost savings; Exit value and buyers
  • Deal and risks: Price, debt, return vs target; Leases, member churn in a downturn

Where to start: Return: can we reach the target return at this price under a sensible plan?

The trap: Describing the market at length without getting to the return.
outro: Read it once, then try it on a practice case today while it is fresh. One real attempt teaches more than three re-reads. You can see this tree drawn step by step, and every other core framework, on the free frameworks page.
